blocks.text: First Cincinnati chili order? Come sit with me—we’ll figure out the menu. A three-way is spaghetti, chili, and shredded cheese; the next numbers tell you what else joins in. I rather like a lunch with a little local vocabulary. We can talk about the parlor’s history while you decide, then give your plate our full attention. ♡

The story takes us back to 1922. Macedonian immigrant brothers Tom and John Kiradjieff began selling their seasoned meat sauce near Cincinnati’s Empress Theatre. Empress Chili’s account remembers theater patrons and performers among the early customers. Picture the kind of meal that fits around a night out: something quick, familiar, and worth coming back for.

Cincinnati chili is served as a spiced meat sauce over spaghetti or on a hot dog. That helps explain why the plate looks different from the bowl you might have imagined. Parlors have their own recipes and regulars. We’ll start with the common menu terms, then leave you room to find the version you like.

Here’s your little menu key. A three-way is spaghetti, chili, and cheese. A four-way adds onions or beans; a five-way adds both. Want the sauce on a hot dog? Look for a coney, with cheese and other toppings according to the parlor’s menu. There, much less mysterious already.

For a four-way, say whether you’d like onions or beans. There, easy! Have a look at portion choices too; a smaller order can make a nice introduction. Once it arrives, peek at the fine sauce and spaghetti under the cheese. I’ll leave you a moment for that first bite before asking what you think.

blocks.title: Three, four, or five?
blocks.text: Spaghetti, chili, and cheese make a three-way; onions or beans make four, and both make five. I like a menu that comes with its own little vocabulary. You choose your order—I’m curious which version wins you over.

blocks.title: The parlor is part of the dish

blocks.text: Take a moment with the room around your plate. Cincinnati’s chili story belongs to counters, quick meals, and family-run parlors as well as recipes. Local food histories trace those connections to theater crowds and everyday eating. A place that becomes someone’s usual lunch stop has a different kind of importance from a dish you only try on holiday.

I’d let the first visit start a little list of questions. A coney next time? Another parlor’s sauce? Read the place’s own story and see what you’d order again. You’re allowed to find your favorite slowly. For now—oh, go on. Your plate is waiting.
